Appendix A C Feature Handling Algorithms

This section presents the representative C feature handler — Conditional Compilation — that augments a CICFG with additional interprocedural edges for a language construct whose execution targets are indirect, deferred, or runtime-resolved. The pseudocode algorithms for the remaining six C feature handlers (Function Pointers, Dynamic Linking, Inline Assembly, Macros to Function Calls, Goto Statements, and Setjmp/Longjmp) follow the same template and are provided in our artifact package.

A-A Conditional Compilation

Description.

Conditional compilation materializes configuration-dependent control-flow that a single preprocessed build cannot cover: each #ifdef, #ifndef, #if, #else, #endif family selects a mutually exclusive code region, and statements that are syntactically present in the source may be excised — or, conversely, only become reachable — under a particular build configuration. A standard CICFG built from a single preprocessed view therefore systematically loses statements and edges contributed by alternative branches, which biases every downstream reachability/taint computation.

Algorithm 3 repairs this in three steps. (1) Detection (line 3). For every input file, the expert panel is asked a YES/NO question on whether preprocessor branching is present; files without any directive are skipped to avoid spending LLM budget on regular C code. (2) Branch enumeration (line 3). On a positive file, the panel returns two structured lists: stmts — statements that exist only inside a particular branch, each tagged with its source line and text — and edges — feasible control-flow edges between lines, each tagged with the branch it belongs to. The panel produces this view jointly across all branches, including ones that the active build configuration would have hidden. (3) CICFG augmentation (lines 3–3). Each branch-guarded statement is materialized as a CICFG node tagged "feat":"condcomp", and each enumerated edge is materialized between the corresponding source/destination lines, additionally tagged with its branch identifier so that later analyses can reason per configuration (intra-branch edges) or across configurations (inter-branch edges) on the same graph. The handler returns the list of touched files and a boolean signaling whether new edges were introduced, which feeds back into the controller’s worklist.

Illustrating example.

On this example, the detection step (line 3) returns YES because two #ifdef directives are present (_MSC_VER and __aarch64__). The branch-enumeration step (line 3) yields two branch-guarded statements — the <intrin.h> include at L2 (gated by _MSC_VER) and the AArch64 NEON computation at L10 (gated by __aarch64__) — plus the corresponding intra-branch edges (e.g., L8→\toL10→\toL11 inside the AArch64 branch) and the inter-branch fall-through L11→\toL12 that re-joins the unconditional control flow. The augmentation step inserts L2 and L10 as new condcomp nodes (so neither statement is silently dropped under the “other” configuration) and adds the listed edges with their branch tags, so a downstream taint analysis traversing main can reach the NEON intrinsic regardless of which configuration the developer’s local build happens to select.

Appendix B Python Feature Handling Algorithms

This section presents the representative Python feature handler — First-Class Functions — that augments a CICFG with additional interprocedural edges for a language construct whose execution targets are indirect, deferred, or runtime-resolved. The pseudocode algorithms for the remaining five Python feature handlers (Dynamic Typing, Decorators, Lambda Expressions, Reflection, and Dynamic Imports) follow the same template and are provided in our artifact package.

B-A First-class functions

Description.

First-class functions enable higher-order control flow: a function value is passed into another function and invoked indirectly via a parameter, so the callee name is not syntactically present at the invocation site and a call graph that only resolves direct calls silently drops the entire higher-order edge.

Algorithm 4 restores these edges in two stages. (1) Per-file extraction (AnalyzeFirstClassFunctions). The expert panel first answers a YES/NO probe on whether the file uses functions-as-values; on a positive answer, it returns every concrete passing site as a tuple ⟨𝑝𝑎𝑠𝑠𝑒𝑑_𝑓𝑢𝑛𝑐,𝑟𝑒𝑐𝑒𝑖𝑣𝑒𝑟_𝑓𝑢𝑛𝑐,\langle\mathit{passed\_func},\mathit{receiver\_func}, 𝑟𝑒𝑐𝑒𝑖𝑣𝑒𝑟_𝑝𝑎𝑟𝑎𝑚,𝑐𝑎𝑙𝑙_𝑙𝑖𝑛𝑒⟩\mathit{receiver\_param},\mathit{call\_line}\rangle, where passed_func is the user-defined function being passed as a value, receiver_func is the higher-order function it is passed into, and receiver_param is the formal parameter inside receiver_func that will receive it. (2) Higher-order resolution (ResolveHigherOrderFlow). For each passing site, the analysis enters the body of receiver_func and asks the panel for two things: call_lines — every line at which receiver_param is invoked as a callable — and forward_sites — every line at which receiver_param is forwarded onward as an argument to a further function gg via some formal parameter g_param. Each call line yields a new CICFG edge from that line to the entry of passed_func, annotated as first-class; each forward site causes the analysis to recurse into gg with ⟨𝑝𝑎𝑠𝑠𝑒𝑑​_​𝑓𝑢𝑛𝑐,g,g​_​p​a​r​a​m⟩\langle\mathit{passed\_func},g,g\_param\rangle, so a value that traverses several higher-order layers is still chased to its eventual invocation. A visited set guards against revisits in the presence sof mutual or cyclic forwarding, and the routine returns whether any new edge was added so the controller knows whether to re-run dependent feature handlers.

Illustrating example.

On this example, the per-file extraction yields a single passing-site tuple ⟨square,my_map,func,L11⟩\langle\texttt{square},\texttt{my\_map},\texttt{func},\mathrm{L11}\rangle. The higher-order resolution then enters my_map’s body and the panel identifies call_lines={L4}\texttt{call\_lines}{=}\{\mathrm{L4}\} (because func is invoked as func(i) at L4) and forward_sites=∅\texttt{forward\_sites}{=}\emptyset (func is not passed onward). The handler therefore inserts a single CICFG edge from L4 of my_map to the entry of square, annotated {"first-class": "func->square"}, making the higher-order call func(i)→\,\to\,square explicit for downstream reachability and taint analyses. Had square been forwarded through one or more wrapper layers before reaching its invocation, the recursive ResolveHigher- OrderFlow call would have followed it through each layer until a call_line was found.

Appendix C Java Feature Handling Algorithms

This section presents the representative Java feature handler — Polymorphism (i.e., polymorphic virtual dispatch on member methods) — that augments a CICFG with additional interprocedural edges for a language construct whose execution targets are indirect, deferred, or runtime-resolved. The pseudocode algorithms for the remaining four Java feature handlers (Reflection, Lambda Expressions, Dynamic Proxies, and Dynamic Class Loading) follow the same template and are provided in our artifact package.

C-A Polymorphism

Description.

Java polymorphic method calls on an interface-typed or base-class-typed receiver (i.e., invokeinterface/invokevirtual bytecodes) are resolved at runtime against the receiver’s dynamic type, not its declared static type. A purely syntactic call graph that links a callsite only to the method declared on the static type therefore systematically misses every concrete override, breaking cross-procedural reachability and dropping data-flow paths that traverse the dispatched body.

Algorithm 5 reconstructs these dispatched edges in three steps. (1) Virtual-callsite extraction (DetectVirtualCalls / ExtractVirtualCalls). For every method m∈Fm\in F, the expert panel first answers a YES/NO probe on whether mm contains a polymorphic dispatch site, and on a positive answer it returns one record per callsite, schema ¡call_line, recv_expr, recv_var, static_recv_type, method_name, param_types, ret_type¿. The signature sig is then derived from (method_name, param_types, ret_type) so it can be looked up uniformly inside the class table CC. (2) Candidate dynamic-type set. The handler tries to bound the dynamic type of recv_var as tightly as soundness allows: if a points-to map 𝒫​𝒯\mathcal{PT} is available, it queries PointsToTypes(𝒫​𝒯,m,recv_var\mathcal{PT},m,\texttt{recv\_var}); otherwise it falls back to Class Hierarchy Analysis, taking every subtype of static_recv_type from CC as a candidate. The candidate set may then be pruned by RefineTypesLLM, which inspects local evidence (e.g., new T(...) allocations and instanceof guards) to drop infeasible types, but only when this strictly shrinks the set — never enlarges it. (3) Per-target edge insertion (ResolveImpl + UpdateCICFGEdge). For each candidate type TT, ResolveImpl walks the override chain (Overrides(C,T,sigC,T,\texttt{sig}), falling back to the first declaration in TT’s super-chain) to identify the concrete implementation that runtime virtual dispatch would actually pick; the handler then inserts a paired call edge (callsite line →\to callee entry) and return edge (callee return →\to callsite line), both annotated {"poly":"virtual","recv":T0,"sig":sig}. The is_updated flag and start_methods list propagate to the controller so that this handler — which is propagation-marked (Y) — can be re-run after dependent feature handlers (e.g., reflective allocation) widen the candidate set.

Illustrating example.

On this example, step (1) returns one virtual-callsite record for run, with call_line=L20, recv_var=sink, static_recv_type=Sink, and signature write(String):void. Step (2) yields the candidate set {FileSink,NetSink}\{\texttt{FileSink},\texttt{NetSink}\} — either because points-to evidence flows the two allocations on L15 forward through choose’s return into sink, or, in the absence of points-to information, because CHA enumerates every subtype of Sink. The optional RefineTypesLLM prune leaves the set unchanged here (no instanceof guard rules either type out). Step (3) then resolves each candidate to its concrete override — FileSink.write(String) (entry/return at L6) and NetSink. write(String) (entry/return at L10) — and inserts two paired call/return edges from L20 to each entry/return, both annotated {"poly": "virtual", "recv": "Sink", "sig": "write(String):void"}. Downstream taint analysis traversing run can now reach both println sites at L6 and L10 from data, instead of stopping at the unresolved Sink.write declaration on L3.
